title: Rules for a Flat World: Why Humans Invented Law and How to Reinvent It for a Complex Global Economy
pub: Oxford University Press (paperback ed. 2020 with new prologue; ISBN 9780199916528)
author: Gillian K. Hadfield

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source summary contains no title, description, key points or quotations, so there is insufficient evidence to assess its position relative to the cluster proposition.

mo.t: Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier

kp.k: Existing legal infrastructure struggles with global economic complexity
kp.d: The publisher's description attributes to Hadfield the argument that existing legal rules cannot adequately support global integration because they are too slow, expensive and geographically limited. This is a summary of the book's thesis, not an empirical finding demonstrated in the supplied page or a specific prediction about AI.
qs: Gillian Hadfield argues that the legal rules that currently guide global integration are no longer working.

They are too slow, costly, and localized for increasingly complex advanced economies, and fail to address issues such as poverty, instability, and oppression for the billions living in the developing world.

kp.k: Digital networks create new demands on legal institutions
kp.d: The publisher frames deeply embedded global supply chains and digital platforms as sources of economic interdependence that create opportunities but also challenges for stability and shared prosperity. In his endorsement, Shane Greenstein identifies contract enforcement, intellectual-property piracy and trade secrets as particular legal challenges associated with digitized supply chains; the page supplies no underlying case evidence.
qs: Global supply chains are now deeply embedded, and digital platforms connect almost everyone in complex networks of data and exchange.
This "flat world" is one of tremendous possibility, but it also poses challenges to stability and shared prosperity.
Modes for enforcing contracts had to change, and governments and private actors continue to experiment with responses to piracy of intellectual property and trade secrets.

kp.k: Legal reform should build more agile infrastructure
kp.d: The publisher presents Hadfield's recommendation as redesigning rules and legal infrastructure to support complex societies and economic interdependence. It places this proposal within a historical account of law's relationship to economic and social prosperity, rather than reporting measured outcomes from a particular reform.
qs: Hadfield proposes a new set of rules that enhance complex societies and economic interdependence and makes the case for building a more agile infrastructure.
In this paperback edition, she presents a new prologue to her sweeping historical overview and vision of the relationship between law and economic and social prosperity.

kp.k: Markets and competition feature in proposed legal redesign
kp.d: The contents explicitly distinguish markets for lawyers from markets for rules. Richard Susskind's endorsement characterizes Hadfield's prescription as greater investment, innovation and competition in legal services, while Colin Rule endorses opening the legal system to market-driven innovation. These are attributed descriptions and endorsements, not evidence that market reforms have achieved the proposed benefits; the page does not specify professional-rule changes.
qs: Chapter 9: Markets for lawyers Chapter 10: Markets for rules
She calls for greater investment, innovation, and competition in legal services and, crucially, challenges lawyers and policymakers to think very differently about the future role of law in society.
Hadfield makes clear that our increasingly wired world requires a new justice system, and opening the legal system to market-driven innovation is the best way to get there.

kp.k: Lower-income countries need context-sensitive legal infrastructure
kp.d: Beyond the publisher's concern with poverty, instability and oppression, Sam Muller's endorsement argues that justice systems' design and production mechanisms are deficient and advocates greater use of markets, particularly where lower-income countries are encouraged to copy Western models. Innocent Chukwuma separately connects the book's debate to African legal architecture inherited from colonialism and removed from daily life. These are endorsers' views, with no quantified access-to-justice findings supplied.
qs: not only do most justice systems not deliver the value they could and should, the design and production machine for getting them to deliver that value is also broken.

For the sake of billions of our fellow global citizens and their aspirations we must open up to using markets more as 'problem solving engines', in particular in the lower income countries that are being told to mirror the models that have been used in the West.
This debate is very germane in Africa still reeling under colonially inspired legal architecture far removed from the daily life of the people.

kp.k: Machine learning raises governance complexity, not staffing predictions
kp.d: John Seely Brown's endorsement uses autonomous vehicles governed by machine learning and cross-border cloud computing as examples of emerging legal complexity requiring institutional innovation. This is the page's explicit machine-learning connection: it concerns governance of technology, not demonstrated automation of lawyers' tasks or predictions about legal employment, pricing or firm structures.
qs: Here in Silicon Valley we pride ourselves on producing radical technological innovations paying but little attention to the messy but critical legal and social issues that require equally radical innovation in our legal systems.
autonomous vehicles governed by machine learning algorithms or cloud computing that crosses so many international boundaries that governance issues become almost unfathomable.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The supplied publisher page contains no concrete author-attributed claim about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: The document is a book description, table of contents, author biography and collection of endorsements, rather than the book itself. OUP's description attributes to Hadfield a broader argument that globalization and technological change have made existing legal infrastructure inadequate and require more agile rules. This is not an AI-specific prediction about legal work, employment or markets. The mention of machine-learning-governed autonomous vehicles occurs in John Seely Brown's endorsement, not in supplied text by Hadfield, and should not be converted into an author-attributed AI claim.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence for an AI-specific legal-services claim is supplied.
pts.d: The page characterizes the book as an interdisciplinary synthesis and historical overview, but supplies no AI performance data, benchmarks, legal-service deployment cases or measured market effects. Endorsements and the author's AI-related affiliations are not evidence of an AI-driven change in legal services.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI adoption timeline or conditional forecast is stated.
pts.d: The broader institutional argument describes a present mismatch between legal rules and increasingly complex, globally integrated economies. The supplied page does not state when AI might transform legal services or identify conditions under which that transformation would occur. Publication and edition dates are not prediction horizons.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The broader argument concerns advanced economies and developing-world populations, without identifying AI-specific effects on legal providers or clients.
pts.d: OUP's description presents existing rules as too slow, expensive and geographically restricted for advanced economies and inadequate to address poverty, instability and oppression in the developing world. It does not identify AI-driven effects on particular lawyer roles, law-firm segments, in-house departments or alternative legal service providers. These broad institutional concerns should not be recast as demonstrated AI cost savings or AI-enabled access to justice.
